name: Esther Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive for Kestrel Drinks, delivering beer kegs, crates and soft drinks to pubs and restaurants around the county. I'm in by six, load up, and do about twelve drops, rolling kegs down into cellars through the hatch in the pavement. I'm still slower than the others on the cellar drops, and my arms ache by Thursday. I love the pub landlords, though, they're characters.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Tomas, who's a joiner, making kitchens and staircases for a small firm. We're at chapel most Sundays, and my mum lives two streets away. Money's tight, maybe two or three weeks saved, because Tomas's work is up and down. I use AI every day, for my budget, for planning Tomas's quotes, and for a little idea I've got about cleaning beer lines for pubs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic. I'd tell the other drivers to try it for the boring paperwork anyway. Online I'd post about how I use it for budgeting, because people ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worries don't change. Pubs keep closing, Kestrel Drinks lost two big accounts last year, and my partner Tomas's work goes quiet every January. There aren't many driving jobs round here that aren't nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and get my cellar drops quicker so I'm not the slow one. I'd start my beer line cleaning idea on Saturdays, because landlords keep telling me their lines are dirty. I'd use AI to work out prices and write a little leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit impatient. I want to build something, not just get by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the beer line cleaning idea.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every pub has pipes running from the kegs to the taps, and they need cleaning every week or two, or the beer tastes off. Lots of landlords hate doing it. With a bit of kit, maybe four hundred pounds' worth, I could do it for them on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the four hundred pounds come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the problem, with almost nothing saved. I'd sell my old bike and put in a bit each week. I wouldn't borrow, my dad always said debt is a trap.

say: AI is still **useful**, just not magic.
Other drivers should try it for the **boring paperwork**.
I'd post about using AI for **budgeting**.
think: My worries stay the same: **pubs closing** and lost accounts.
Tomas's work goes **quiet every January**, and local jobs are mostly nights.
do: Speed up my **cellar drops** so I'm not the slow one.
Start a **beer line cleaning** service on Saturdays.
Use AI to **price it** and write a leaflet.
S0.quote: Pubs keep closing, Kestrel Drinks lost two big accounts last year, and my partner Tomas's work goes quiet every January.
fieldNote: Pressures exist without AI: **pub closures** and her partner's seasonal work.
Enterprising: sees a **side business** in her customers' dirty beer lines.
Traditional values show in **refusing debt**, following her father.

steps.text: Speed up cellar drops on the Kestrel round
Start a Saturday beer line cleaning service for local pubs
Use AI to price the service and write a leaflet
Sell her old bike to fund four hundred pounds of kit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to learn. At work I'd show the others how the new ordering apps work. I'd say it at chapel too, that we shouldn't be scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my driving is safe for a few years. No robot is rolling kegs into a cellar down a slippery hatch any time soon. But Kestrel's office will shrink, and the landlords will order through apps, so fewer reps visit the pubs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every system Kestrel brings in, first. I'd grow the line cleaning to two or three Saturdays a month, and offer it to the pubs on my round. I'd also help Tomas use AI to do his kitchen drawings and quotes faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little bit worried for the office ladies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer reps would visit pubs. What does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm the only face from Kestrel that a lot of landlords see. That's a good place to be, if I use it. They'll tell me what they need, and I can sell them my line cleaning too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kestrel would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline in accounts, who chases late payers by phone. She's 58 and she's brilliant, but software will chase invoices without needing a lunch break. I'd hate to see her go.

say: This is a **chance** for people willing to learn.
I'd show the others the **new ordering apps**.
We **shouldn't be scared**, I'd say at chapel.
think: No robot is **rolling kegs** into cellars any time soon.
Kestrel's **office will shrink** and fewer reps will visit pubs.
do: Grow **line cleaning** to two or three Saturdays a month.
Help Tomas use AI for **kitchen quotes**.
feel: **Excited**, a little worried for office staff.
S1.quote: No robot is rolling kegs into a cellar down a slippery hatch any time soon.
fieldNote: Sees herself becoming the **only Kestrel face** landlords meet, and plans to use it.
Worries for **Pauline in accounts**, a named older colleague.
Spreads her AI habits into her **partner's joinery** work.

steps.text: Learn Kestrel's new ordering apps before other drivers
Offer beer line cleaning to pubs on her Kestrel round
Set up AI kitchen drawings and quotes for Tomas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, but people who work and adapt will find a place. I'd say government should help with training, not just hand out money. And I'd tell the drivers to start something on the side now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, by 2031 robots roll the kegs and drive the truck, and my job's gone. My line cleaning business might go too, if a robot can clean lines. Tomas's joinery might last a bit longer, because every old house is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the next three years to build the line cleaning into a proper little business, while it still needs hands. I'd use AI to run the bookings, invoices and marketing. I'd also look at training to install and service cellar robots, because if pubs get them, someone has to look after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I've got a plan. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're planning a business that robots might also take. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. But it's three or four years of income, and the customers I build will trust me with whatever comes next. The landlords would rather ring me, Esther, than a robot company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum not to worry and that we'll pray about it. And then I'd go home and do a spreadsheet, because faith and planning go together.

say: People who **work and adapt** will find a place.
Government should help with **training**, not hand out money.
Drivers should start **something on the side** now.
think: By **2031** robots roll kegs and drive, and my job's gone.
Even my **line cleaning** might go if robots can do it.
do: Build line cleaning into a **proper business** over three years.
Train to **service cellar robots** if pubs get them.
S2.quote: The landlords would rather ring me, Esther, than a robot company.
fieldNote: Uses the **three-year gap** to build hands-on income before robots arrive.
Sees **trust with customers** as what carries over to her next job.
Combines **faith and planning**, praying then doing a spreadsheet.
Thin savings keep her **anxious** despite a clear plan.

steps.text: Grow beer line cleaning into a registered small business
Run bookings, invoices and marketing through AI tools
Train to install and service cellar robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd tell the young drivers at Kestrel to stop moaning and pick something. I'd share what I'm doing online, so people see it can work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, eight years to the robots gives me time to have the line cleaning running properly and still drive. I'd be 35, maybe with a child. That's a lot to juggle, but I like a lot to juggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the line cleaning to most weekends within two years, then drop to four days at Kestrel. I'd save from the business for a small van of my own. Around 2031, when AGI comes, I'd use it to run the whole business side so I can stay on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. Nervous about money, but good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a child. How does that fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas and I want one in the next few years. With five years to AGI, I think we'd still go ahead. My mum would help with childcare, she's already offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money risk you're nervous about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van. A second-hand van would be about five thousand pounds, and I don't borrow. So it all depends on saving from the business, and one quiet winter could set me back months.

say: Five years is enough to get ready **if you start now**.
Young drivers should **stop moaning** and pick something.
I'd **share my plan** online so people see it work.
think: Eight years to robots gives me time to get **line cleaning running**.
At **35**, maybe with a child, I'd be juggling a lot.
do: Grow line cleaning to **most weekends** within two years.
Save for a **five-thousand-pound van** without borrowing.
S3.quote: A second-hand van would be about five thousand pounds, and I don't borrow.
fieldNote: Time lets her **combine** driving, a business and a child.
Her **no-debt rule** slows the plan and keeps money tight.
Family support from her **mother** underpins the child plan.

steps.text: Run beer line cleaning most weekends within two years
Save five thousand pounds for a second-hand van
Plan a first child with Tomas, with her mum helping
Hand bookings and invoices to AI when AGI arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real opportunity, and anyone willing to work can be ready. I'd be telling everyone at chapel and at Kestrel to start planning. Online I'd be the cheerful one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I'd be 40 when robot trucks arrive, and I plan to be running my own business long before that. The thinking AI in 2036 would do my admin and probably help me grow. That sounds good to me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving at Kestrel for two or three years and build the line cleaning slowly, with no debt. I'd buy a van once I've saved for it, then go full time on the business. Later I'd add cellar maintenance and maybe take on a helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Excited. The money's tight now, but the road ahead looks fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, a bit. He's a craftsman and he doesn't like computers. The robots won't make bespoke staircases, but the AI will draw them, so my partner Tomas should learn the design tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I've got his stubbornness and my mum's head for numbers. He'd be proud, I think. He always wanted to run his own garage and never did.

say: Everyone at chapel and Kestrel should **start planning**.
think: I'd be **running my own business** long before robot trucks arrive.
Thinking AI in **2036** would do my admin and help me grow.
do: Drive at Kestrel **two or three years** while building the business.
Buy a **van** once saved, then go full time.
Add **cellar maintenance** and maybe a helper.
feel: **Calm** and excited, though money is tight now.
S4.quote: The robots won't make bespoke staircases, but the AI will draw them, so my partner Tomas should learn the design tools.
fieldNote: With ten years she expects to **gain**, not lose, from AI.
Calm despite thin savings because her plan has **time to work**.
Worries mainly for her **partner's reluctance** with computers.

steps.text: Keep driving the Kestrel pub round for two or three years
Build the beer line cleaning business slowly with no debt
Buy a van with saved cash, then go full time
Get Tomas using AI design tools for staircases

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots could take the cellar work before my business is strong enough. What would help is cheap, practical training for small business owners, and small grants for kit, not loans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the pubs. They're where people in a village meet. If they close, it's not just my round, it's everyone's Friday night.

portrait: Esther, 27, delivers **kegs and crates** to pubs for Kestrel Drinks, still slow on cellar drops.
She lives with joiner Tomas, goes to **chapel**, and refuses to borrow money.
She uses AI daily and plans a **beer line cleaning** business for pubs.
Traditional and enterprising, she favours **training over handouts**.
With ten years she's calm and expects to **run her own business**; with two, she's anxious.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as robots could take cellar work before her business is ready.
